name: Kang-Petrov Arms KPA-16 'Flatline'
description:
The KPA-16 is Kang-Petrov's entry-level AR-pattern carbine chambered in 5.56mm Combat Standard brass-cased ammunition, built around a mid-length direct impingement gas system and a 16-inch chrome-lined barrel. The receiver is stamped from Slagworks-grade recycled alloy — not as pretty as billet, but it takes abuse without cracking. The adjustable six-position stock is polymer-composite, the handguard runs a modest M-LOK rail layout, and the trigger is a mil-spec two-stage unit that breaks at roughly 2.1 kilograms. It cycles reliably on standard-pressure loads and most surplus ammunitiin the Gray Zone markets push, though it prefers clean brass and will let you know with a stovepipe when you feed it the really cheap stuff.

The KPA-16 occupies the uncomfortable middle ground between the KP-19 pistol family and KP's own AK-pattern rifles — lighter than the KPR line, more modular, but demanding slightly more maintenance discipline from its operators. It sells primarily to Tier 1–2 buyers who've scraped together enough Quanta to move up from pistol-only carry: small business owners in the outer GLMZ rings, cooperative security details, and the kind of mid-tier fixers who need something with reach but can't afford Arcturus Defense Solutions catalog prices. Slagworks markets it as 'the working person's fighting rifle,' and for once the advertising isn't entirely dishonest.

A well-used KPA-16 tells a story in its finish. The phosphate coating on the barrel goes first — usually around the gas block where operators have burned their hands enough times that they wrap it in salvaged heat tape. The lower receiver develops a characteristic wear pattern at the mag well from the repetitive slap-and-rock of curved 5.56 mags that don't quite want to seat like a KPR mag does. Street armorers in the GLMZ's outer boroughs keep KPA-16 parts in stock because the rifle has been around long enough that a whole ecosystem of shade-tree repair has grown up around it. Some of those rifles have passed through four or five hands and still run.

tactical_use: The KPA-16 is a general-purpose defensive carbine best suited to engagements from 0 to 300 meters where the operator needs more stopping authority than a pistol but doesn't want to carry the weight of a full-length rifle. Operators typically run it with a red dot or low-power variable optic, a weapon light, and a sling — simple loadout, nothing exotic. It rewards disciplined fire and penalizes spray-and-pray operators with heat buildup at the gas block. The mid-length gas system softens recoil slightly compared to carbine-length variants, making follow-up shots more manageable for less experienced shooters.
cultural_context: In GLMZ's outer boroughs, the KPA-16 is what people buy when they've decided a pistol isn't enough anymore. It doesn't carry the prestige of the KPR line's Soviet-lineage brutalism or the tactical-operator cachet of Arcturus hardware, but it's everywhere — co-op defense rotations, small-crew security details, the occasional the Gray Zone worker collective that pooled resources after a bad run-in with Excluded zone incursions. Mids who carry one sometimes feel the need to apologize for it. the Gray Zone workers who carry one feel no such need.
story_hooks: A KPA-16 with a cracked lower receiver is found at a crime scene in a Tessera Corponation transit corridor — the serial has been ground off, but the wear patterns match a specific the Gray Zone worker collective's armory that was raided three weeks ago.

An outer-borough armorer is offering KPA-16 builds using parts that are just slightly too well-machined to be factory Slagworks — someone is running a gray-market parts supply chain, and the quality is good enough that a KP quality-control investigator has gone missing looking into it.
